planting.note: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix; Alocasia melo is particularly susceptible to root rot, so never allow the pot to sit in standing water. Maintain warm temperatures above 60°F and high humidity to prevent crispy leaf margins.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix, allowing the top inch or two to dry before watering again. Alocasia melo is a slow-growing species prized for its extraordinarily thick, stiff, matte, blue-gray-green leaves with a rough, pebbled, almost armored surface texture, earning it the nickname Rhino Skin among collectors for a look unlike the glossy, thin-textured foliage of most other alocasias. Its compact size and dramatically textured leaves make it a striking specimen for a bright windowsill or grow-light shelf rather than a large floor plant. It is more tolerant of brief dry spells than many alocasias thanks to its thick, water-storing leaves, but still resents both soggy soil and prolonged drought; keep warm, humid, and out of direct sun, which can scorch the leaf surface.

planting.note: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix; Maharani is particularly susceptible to root rot, so never allow the pot to sit in standing water. Maintain warm temperatures above 60°F and high humidity.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix, allowing the top inch or two to dry before watering again. Maharani, also sold as Grey Dragon, is a compact hybrid alocasia related to Alocasia melo with thick, stiff, dusty grey-green leaves showing the same rough, pebbled, almost armored texture, but in a smaller-growing, more clumping form well suited to a windowsill or grow-light shelf. Its dwarf stature and slow growth make it a good choice for collectors with limited bright-light space, and it tolerates brief dry spells slightly better than thinner-leaved alocasias thanks to its water-storing foliage. Keep it warm and humid, out of direct sun, which scorches the leaf surface, and repot only when clearly rootbound, since alocasias generally prefer being slightly snug in their pots.

common_name: Mini Mark Phalaenopsis (Miniature Yellow-Spotted Moth Orchid)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in zone 9; Mini Mark cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Grow in slatted orchid pots or clear plastic pots in coarse orchid bark media with excellent drainage. Water thoroughly once or twice per week, allowing the media to dry partially between waterings.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — an east or shaded south window suits it well, since direct sun burns the leaves and dim conditions reduce reblooming. Mini Mark is a compact, miniature phalaenopsis hybrid bearing smaller flowers than standard moth orchids, in creamy yellow-green overlaid with fine reddish-brown spots and stripes, held on a shorter, more manageable spike well suited to a crowded windowsill or small growing space. Its compact overall size and modest root system make it a good choice for narrow spaces where full-sized phalaenopsis are unwieldy. Never remove a green flower spike after bloom, since reblooming often occurs from side branches; repot every one to two years in fresh bark once the old media has decomposed.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Fang is drought-tolerant and rots quickly in wet or dense soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix. Fang is a striking Kalanchoe beharensis hybrid with felted, silvery-bronze, wavy-edged leaves lined underneath with rows of blunt, tooth-like protrusions that give the plant its name, a novelty texture distinct from the smoother succulents most people grow. It develops a sturdy, upright, woody-stemmed form over time, similar to its parent species, and tolerates the same neglect and irregular watering typical of other kalanchoe succulents. Water only when the soil has dried out completely, since it is highly susceptible to root and stem rot in constantly moist conditions, and give it the brightest light available for the most compact, well-colored growth.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; Pink Butterflies is a sterile hybrid that produces plantlets along the leaf margins but not viable seed, so it spreads only where those plantlets are allowed to root.

directions: Grow in bright light, including some direct sun, in well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only when the soil has dried out. Pink Butterflies is a variegated, sterile hybrid related to Mother of Thousands, with cream-and-green mottled leaf centers edged in pink-blushed margins lined with small plantlets that root readily wherever they touch soil, giving the whole plant a soft pastel coloring the wild species lacks. Because this hybrid does not set viable seed, it lacks the aggressive self-sowing weediness of its parent species and is considered a safer choice for gardens near natural areas in frost-free zones, though the marginal plantlets still root and spread if left to fall on open soil. Bright light produces the strongest pink coloring; low light causes the plant to green out and stretch.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Hobbit jade plant is extremely drought-tolerant and rots quickly in wet or dense soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix. Hobbit is a curly-leaved jade plant sport closely related to Gollum, with thick, tubular, jade-green leaves that curl tightly back on themselves along their length rather than forming Gollum's open, suction-cup-tipped trumpets, giving Hobbit a denser, more twisted, almost coral-like texture. Like other jade plant cultivars it branches into a sturdy, tree-like miniature shrub over years and is sometimes grown and shaped as informal bonsai material for its naturally gnarled, woody habit. It tolerates irregular watering and low humidity typical of most homes; water only when the soil has dried out fully, and provide the brightest light available for the most compact growth and best leaf color.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Dondo requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of standing water in the center of the rosette.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade. Dondo forms tight rosettes of thick, powdery blue-green leaves with distinctly ruffled, wavy margins that pick up a pink to coral blush at the tips and edges in bright light and cooler temperatures, giving the rosette a frilled, decorative outline compared to smoother-edged echeveria hybrids. Like other echeveria it needs sharp drainage and infrequent, deep watering, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings, and makes an excellent container or rock garden specimen in warm, dry conditions. In zone 9a grow it outdoors in a well-drained bed or pot through the warm season and protect from prolonged winter wet and hard freezes.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Ramillette requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of standing water in the center of the rosette.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade. Ramillette forms small, tight, compact rosettes of pale blue-green leaves that blush rosy pink to coral along the tips and margins with bright light and cooler weather, staying dense and low-growing rather than elongating on a stem the way some echeveria hybrids do with age. Its compact scale and reliable offsetting habit make it a popular choice for succulent dish gardens, mixed containers, and rock gardens where a small, tidy rosette is wanted. Like other echeveria it needs sharp drainage and infrequent, deep watering, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings; in zone 9a grow it outdoors in a well-drained bed or pot and protect from prolonged winter wet.

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or elevated container in bright light to part shade in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; the trailing stems and closely packed leaves are very brittle and drop easily when handled or bumped.

directions: Grow in a hanging basket or elevated container in bright light to part shade in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, watering only when the soil has dried out. Burrito is closely related to the better-known Burro's Tail (Sedum morganianum) but carries shorter, more rounded, tightly overlapping blue-green leaves without Burro's Tail's longer, pointed tip, giving its trailing stems a denser, chunkier, bead-like look. Like its relative, the plump leaves store water and detach very easily at the slightest touch, so hang the basket somewhere it will not be brushed against, and use any dropped leaves to start new plants by resting them on top of moist succulent mix. Bright light keeps growth compact; too little light causes the stems to stretch and the leaves to space out unevenly.
